subtopics.title: The Cast of Symbols and the Two Kinds of Growth

questions.question: An interest rate of 7% per annum enters either growth formula as:
options: 1,7 substituted directly for i

questions.question: The one-sentence difference between simple and compound growth is that:
options: Compound growth always uses a bigger rate
Simple interest is calculated on the principal alone; compound interest is calculated on the principal plus all accumulated interest
Simple growth only applies to loans
Compound growth runs for more years

questions.question: In A = P(1 + i)^n, the bracket carries the power n because:
options: The growth factor is applied once per period, each time to a balance that has already grown
n is always the largest number in the question
Powers make the answer bigger, which banks prefer
It is a typesetting habit with no meaning

subtopics.title: Simple Growth — Executing A = P(1 + in)

questions.question: R4 000 at 7% per annum simple interest for 3 years accumulates to:
Inside the bracket of A = 4 000(1 + 0,07 × 3), the correct order of operations gives:
options: 1 + 0,07 = 1,07, then stop

questions.question: The check that confirms a simple-interest answer is:
options: The interest breaks into equal annual payments, each exactly the rate applied to the original principal
The final amount is a round number
The interest grows larger every year
The bracket works out to exactly 1

subtopics.title: Compound Growth — Executing A = P(1 + i)ⁿ

questions.question: R4 000 at 7% per annum compounded annually for 3 years accumulates to:
options: R4 920 exactly

questions.question: Writing A = 4 000(1 + 0,07 × 3) in a question that says 'compounded annually' is wrong because:
options: The principal belongs outside the bracket
It is the simple formula — under compounding, n must be an exponent: 4 000(1,07)³
The rate should have been 7, not 0,07
Nothing is wrong — both forms give the same answer

questions.question: The R60,17 gap between the compound and simple answers is explained by:
options: Rounding the growth factor too early
Interest earned by earlier interest: R19,60 extra in year two and R40,57 extra in year three
Bank charges on the simple account
A slightly higher rate in the compound case

questions.question: When should the growth factor 1,225043 be rounded?
options: Immediately, to 1,23
After every multiplication
Never — rounding is forbidden in finance
Only at the final answer, to two decimals for money

subtopics.title: Choosing the Formula and Working Backwards

questions.question: By the standing convention for this topic, hire purchase is calculated with:
options: Compound interest — A = P(1 + i)^n
Simple interest — A = P(1 + in)
Whichever formula the shop prefers
No interest at all

questions.question: A laptop costs R12 000 on hire purchase over 3 years at 10% p.a. simple interest. The total paid and monthly instalment are:
options: R15 600 total; R433,33 per month
R13 200 total; R366,67 per month
R15 972 total; R443,67 per month
R14 400 total; R400 per month

questions.question: What principal must be deposited at 5% compound interest to reach R8 000 in 3 years?
Which list correctly pairs scenarios with COMPOUND growth?
options: Hire purchase and equal monthly instalments
Any question that mentions a percentage
Inflation, savings compounded annually, population growth
Only questions set inside a bank

subtopics.title: Two Pictures — the Bicycle and the Hens

questions.question: In the two pictures, the bicycle rental stands for simple growth because:
options: Bicycles lose value over time
The payment is calculated on the same original arrangement every time and never changes
Rent is paid monthly instead of yearly
The rent increases every month

questions.question: The aunt's flock of hens grows faster and faster because:
options: Hens lay more eggs in summer
She buys new hens with her salary
Some eggs hatch into new hens that also lay — the growth itself starts producing
The eggs get bigger every year

questions.question: Which everyday situation matches the HEN-COOP picture?
options: A flat R280 rental arriving every month
Paying the same bus fare every morning
A savings account where each year's interest is added to the balance and then earns too
A once-off discount on one price

subtopics.title: The Same R4 000, Built Year by Year

questions.question: Built year by year at 7% compound, R4 000 becomes:
In year two of the compound build, the interest is R299,60 rather than R280 because:
options: The rate rose to 7,49%
7% is now calculated on R4 280 — last year's R280 has joined the balance and earns too
A thirteenth month was counted
R299,60 is a rounding error

questions.question: If both formulas desert you in a test, the year-by-year build is valuable because:
options: It is quicker than the formula
It only works when n is 3
It reconstructs either answer from arithmetic you can always do — a formula is just this build in a hurry
Markers award bonus marks for long methods

subtopics.title: Which Deal Is in Front of You?

questions.question: 'A stove bought on hire purchase over 24 months' is which deal?
options: The hen-coop deal — compound growth
Neither — hire purchase carries no interest
Both formulas apply equally
The bicycle deal — simple interest on the original price

questions.question: Why is inflation a hen-coop (compound) situation?
options: Because each year's price rise lands on top of prices that had already risen
Because inflation only affects food prices
Because the government sets a new rate each year
Because prices never come down

questions.question: The honest warning about compound growth is that:
options: It stops after five years
It works both ways — a gift for savings you own, a burden for debts you owe
It only ever benefits the bank
It is not allowed on loans
